papers.title: A Single-Powder Strategy for LPBF and DED Processing of BCC Nb–Ti–Zr Alloy
papers.abstract: Refractory multi-principal element alloys offer high melting temperatures and compositional flexibility for structural applications under extreme conditions. In the Nb–Ti–Zr ternary system, Zr confers corrosion resistance and a low neutron capture cross-section, while Nb stabilizes the body-centered cubic (BCC) phase across a wide composition space, and Ti, the lightest constituent, lowers the alloy density. Here we report the first additive manufacturing of Nb 25 Ti 20 Zr 55 by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) and laser directed energy deposition (LDED) from a single prealloyed powder. Both routes produced intact builds with sparse pores across much of the processing window, with cracking confined to part of the LPBF range. Electron backscatter diffraction and X-ray diffraction indexed a predominantly body-centered cubic microstructure at Zr contents of 50.4 to 55.5 at.% across both routes. Ti evaporated preferentially, falling 9.5 at.% from the feedstock in LPBF, yet the BCC phase was retained. The LPBF composition was uniform across the processing window. The LDED composition varied with energy density and approached the LPBF value only at the highest energy density. LPBF gave finer grains (96 μm) than LDED (140 μm) at equivalent hardness (H = 2.73 to 2.90 GPa) and Young’s modulus (E = 79 to 83 GPa).

papers.title: Hierarchical Composite Endpoints for Dose Optimization in Early Phase Oncology Trials
papers.abstract: The FDA-initiated Project Optimus has emphasized the need for dose optimization (DO) in oncology drug development, moving beyond the traditional maximum tolerated dose paradigm. Evaluating the balance of benefit and risk is central to DO. In this paper, we propose a novel benefit-risk assessment framework for DO in early-phase oncology trials, utilizing hierarchical composite endpoints (HCEs). The HCE approach enables integration of multiple endpoints within a clinically prioritized hierarchy. Generalized pairwise comparison is then used to compare patient outcomes across candidate dose levels in DO cohorts, providing interpretable metrics to guide dose selection. Our method addresses key practical challenges of existing methods by enabling straightforward, qualitative clinical inputs and integrating various DO-related evidence. The framework also supports uncertainty quantification and sensitivity analysis to ensure robust assessment. Additionally, we extend the HCE method to incorporate pharmacokinetic data through a probabilistic index model, allowing drug exposure to support dose selection. Extensive simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior performance in selecting optimal doses compared to utility-score-based methods, particularly in scenarios requiring careful balancing of efficacy and safety. Application to real-world trial data for DO in HER-2 positive nonsmall cell lung cancer further illustrates the method's practical utility and robustness.

papers.abstract: Encapsulation of the heterocyclic quinoid species, 1,10-phenanthroline-5,6-dione (PDon) was achieved via an enzymatically assisted electrodeposition approach on carbon transducers. The reagentless glucose biosensing methodology took advantage of a layered biopolymer with biocompatible conducting bioink formulation. The PDon mediating layer served as a proton and electron acceptor for FADH 2 glucose oxidase cofactor regeneration. Scanning electron microscopy revealed interesting microstructures on both glassy carbon (GC) and woven fabric carbon cloth (CC) substrates while electrochemical film studies established surface confined behaviour and the expected proton coupled electron transfer process. Quantitative glucose investigations involved differential pulse voltammetry (DPV) and constant potential approaches in phosphate buffer (pH 6.0 and 7.4). DPV studies resulted in sensitivity 1.00 × 10 -7 ± 4.27 × 10 -9 A mmol -1 L (2.0-4.0 mmol L -1 ) and 1.20 × 10 -5 ± 8.64 × 10 -7 A mmol -1 L (1.0-4.95 mmol L -1 ) for GC and CC electrodes respectively, with the latter resulting in limit of detection of 0.55 ± 0.30 mmol L -1 and apparent Michaelis Menton constant, K m ′ = 0.79 ± 0.01 mmol L -1 . The redox behaviour of the CC transducer was found to be intact following > 10 months at 4 °C.

papers.title: Large eddy simulation of unsteady cooling characteristics in triply periodic minimal surface-based transpiration cooling
papers.abstract: Triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) lattices provide a promising architecture for transpiration cooling by promoting uniform near-wall coolant coverage. Although their time-averaged cooling performance has been investigated, the unsteady organization of the wall thermal response and the associated flow structures remains insufficiently understood. In this study, wall-resolved large eddy simulations were performed for diamond and gyroid TPMS transpiration cooling at coolant injection ratios of 9.0% and 18.0%. Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) was applied to the fluctuating wall cooling effectiveness and wall-normal velocity fields to quantify modal energy distributions and identify leading unsteady structures. Results show that, for both lattices, the coolant coverage extended farther downstream at F = 18.0% than at F = 9.0%, while the area-averaged standard deviation of cooling effectiveness differed only slightly between the two conditions. The diamond lattice produced around 20% higher area-averaged cooling effectiveness and a 5% lower relative fluctuation level than the gyroid lattice, indicating more effective and temporally stable wall protection under the present conditions. The POD energy spectra of both TPMS lattices were broadly distributed across multiple modes, with each leading mode accounting for only a limited fraction of the total fluctuation energy. The leading thermal modes were concentrated near the local jet exits of the TPMS lattices, reflecting unsteady coolant discharge and variations in near-wall coverage in the exit region. Their broadband spectra demonstrated that the leading wall thermal response spanned multiple time scales. The instantaneous fields and velocity POD modes further revealed multiscale flow disturbances with streamwise convective organization, and several velocity modes exhibited preferred-frequency peaks.

papers.title: Is Language Doing More of the Reasoning Than We Think
papers.abstract: Language is the dominant interface through which modern frontier models are trained, prompted, evaluated, and asked to expose their reasoning, encouraging the tempting inference that if reasoning quality improves when a model generates more words, language itself is doing the reasoning; however, cross-disciplinary evidence does not support this conclusion in its strongest form: human neuroimaging and lesion studies show that natural-language processing can dissociate from formal logic and mathematics, nonhuman animals exhibit planning and recursive-sequence behavior without human-like language, and model-based reinforcement learning systems plan over nonlinguistic state representations. Synthesizing evidence from cognitive neuroscience, aphasia, numerical cognition, comparative cognition, reinforcement learning, world models, chain-of-thought research, latent reasoning, and mechanistic interpretability, we note that while language can provide exact symbolic labels, relational binding, and external working memory, its use in autoregressive models additionally functions as a computational clock where every generated token adds a forward pass, a writable state, and an opportunity for search or correction - thereby confounding linguistic semantics with sequential compute. We propose three distinct hypotheses - language as substrate, scaffold, or interface - and introduce LDD-6, a Language Dependence Decomposition separating representation, computation, workspace, supervision, coordination, and auditability, alongside a compute-matched causal evaluation protocol to measure when language contributes beyond equivalent latent or nonsemantic computation. Our central conclusion is two-sided: natural language is not a necessary substrate for intelligence, but linguistic externalization is currently an unusually effective cognitive technology for both humans and language models, pointing to a hybrid architecture - latent world modeling and planning beneath an optional, controllable linguistic workspace that supports communication, reflection, supervision, and oversight without forcing every intermediate state through words.

papers.title: Improved printability and performance of functionally graded Inconel 625-GRCop-42 alloy created with directed energy deposition via reactive additive manufacturing
papers.abstract: The integration of high-strength superalloys with high-thermal-conductivity copper alloys is essential for the development of next-generation aerospace propulsion components, such as liquid rocket engine nozzles. However, the fabrication of functionally graded materials (FGMs) between dissimilar metals via directed energy deposition (DED) is significantly challenged by a liquid miscibility gap, leading to severe macro-segregation, elemental variability, and the formation of brittle intermetallic phases. This study presents a novel approach to defect suppression in Inconel 625 (IN625)-GRCop-42 FGMs through the application of reactive additive manufacturing (RAM). Microstructural characterization reveals that RAM inoculation of IN625 powders effectively disrupts the formation of continuous liquid films, which cause solidification cracking, and suppresses the precipitation of the brittle topologically close-packed phases. Compared to conventional IN625-GRCop-42 FGM samples, which exhibited significant elemental segregation and an inconsistent grain morphology driven by the separate solidification of a Cu-lean and Cu-rich liquid, the RAM-modified gradients demonstrate a highly uniform elemental transition, improved microstructural homogeneity, and increased ductility. This work represents a new avenue to modify solidification pathways in this FGM system to produce high-performance, multi-material components for high-heat-flux environments.

papers.title: Is Language Doing More of the Reasoning Than We Think
papers.abstract: Language is the dominant interface through which modern frontier models are trained, prompted, evaluated, and asked to expose their reasoning, encouraging the tempting inference that if reasoning quality improves when a model generates more words, language itself is doing the reasoning; however, cross-disciplinary evidence does not support this conclusion in its strongest form: human neuroimaging and lesion studies show that natural-language processing can dissociate from formal logic and mathematics, nonhuman animals exhibit planning and recursive-sequence behavior without human-like language, and model-based reinforcement learning systems plan over nonlinguistic state representations. Synthesizing evidence from cognitive neuroscience, aphasia, numerical cognition, comparative cognition, reinforcement learning, world models, chain-of-thought research, latent reasoning, and mechanistic interpretability, we note that while language can provide exact symbolic labels, relational binding, and external working memory, its use in autoregressive models additionally functions as a computational clock where every generated token adds a forward pass, a writable state, and an opportunity for search or correction - thereby confounding linguistic semantics with sequential compute. We propose three distinct hypotheses - language as substrate, scaffold, or interface - and introduce LDD-6, a Language Dependence Decomposition separating representation, computation, workspace, supervision, coordination, and auditability, alongside a compute-matched causal evaluation protocol to measure when language contributes beyond equivalent latent or nonsemantic computation. Our central conclusion is two-sided: natural language is not a necessary substrate for intelligence, but linguistic externalization is currently an unusually effective cognitive technology for both humans and language models, pointing to a hybrid architecture - latent world modeling and planning beneath an optional, controllable linguistic workspace that supports communication, reflection, supervision, and oversight without forcing every intermediate state through words.

papers.title: Erosion, Degradation, and Reliability of Next‐Generation Biomedical Internet of Medical Things Devices: Mechanisms, Monitoring, and Predictive Modeling
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Next‐generation biomedical Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) devices such as implantable sensors, wearable systems, and hybrid transcutaneous platforms have radically changed the way we approach healthcare, enabling continuous patient monitoring and real‐time intervention. With the global biomedical IoMT market expected to exceed USD 187 billion by 2028, the question of how long these devices can operate reliably is an urgent concern for engineers and clinicians alike. However, the realization of this potential is blocked by the fact that these devices degrade. Material erosion, corrosion, wear, tribocorrosion, and biologically induced breakdown—all driven by the harsh physiological conditions inside and on the human body—place hard limits on how long a device can safely operate. Unlike traditional implants, IoMT devices include miniature electronics and wireless telemetry into a variety of material interfaces. Such complexity means that failures rarely happen in isolation—different degradation pathways reinforce each other in ways that are hard to predict. This review concentrates on the degradation of IoMT devices at the system level, discussing the underlying failure mechanisms, material selection, surface engineering strategies, and the often‐overlooked topics of packaging and hermetic sealing. We cover electrochemical corrosion, mechanically assisted wear, polymer hydrolysis, biofouling, and additive manufacturing induced surface instabilities for both implantable and wearable systems. Also, existing in vitro, in vivo, and accelerated‐aging test methods are critically evaluated with specific emphasis on their inadequacy in mimicking the coupled long‐term stressors experienced by devices in real life application. In addition to materials and testing, this work addresses the emerging ability of IoMT devices to monitor their own degradation in real‐time, via impedance‐based sensing, embedded electrochemical microsensors, and wireless telemetry to stream device health data to clinicians. We describe how physics‐based models can be combined with data‐driven models to predict remaining useful life (RUL). We discuss the role of machine learning, hybrid degradation frameworks, uncertainty quantification and the explainability requirements imposed by regulators. Finally, we identify the open problems—standardization gaps, unresolved modeling challenges and broader engineering questions—which must be addressed before truly erosion‐aware, self‐monitoring IoMT devices become clinical reality. Our goal is to serve as a complete, technical reference for material scientists, device engineers, and clinicians to design IoMT systems that work and remain durable and safe for long‐term use. A synthesis of available IoMT failure data shows that corrosion and wear combined contribute to more than 45% of device failures, a figure that alone justifies the case for taking degradation‐aware design seriously. The novelty of this review is that it is, to our knowledge, the first to unify these numbers into a single IoMT‐specific framework: it synthesizes findings from 20 primary experimental studies spanning corrosion, wear and tribocorrosion and 48 total references, quantifies that corrosion and wear together account for over 45% of reported device failures, and shows that packaging and interconnect degradation is the single most common precursor to catastrophic failure across the implantable, wearable and hybrid device classes (Section 10).

papers.title: Constrained Bayesian optimization-driven design of a microfluidic particle separator under a pressure-drop limit
Probabilistic Inverse Airfoil Design Using Experimentally-driven Machine Learning Models
papers.abstract: Conventional inverse design methods evaluate the aerodynamics of candidate airfoils using Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations, which are computationally expensive and inherently deterministic, limiting design space exploration and uncertainty quantification. This paper offers an alternative approach by introducing an experimentally-driven surrogate model-based probabilistic inverse formalism, in which both the target quantity of interest and the resulting design are represented as statistical distributions. Notably, the formulation of the target C p is generalized to enable inverse design across multiple operating conditions within a unified framework. Employing stochastic variational inference, the design loop obtains the design distribution by minimizing the symmetrized Kullback–Leibler divergence loss. Inactive subspace analysis is then performed, characterizing the geometric perturbations that have minimal impact on the C p distribution (i.e. the tolerance). The approach leverages the Large Airfoil Model (LAM), an uncertainty-aware machine learning surrogate trained entirely on an experimental dataset, whose accuracy, computational efficiency, and automatic differentiation capability enable rapid optimization. Across three test cases, the framework recovered the target geometries with thickness residuals below 0.5% of maximum thickness. The framework achieved substantial computational savings, requiring under 10.8 minutes for a single design point on a CPU and providing up to a 2.87 × speedup over an equivalent RANS-driven inverse design workflow using SU2, with further gains on a single A100 GPU, requiring only 255 s and 590.83 s for the single- and three-point design cases, respectively.

papers.title: Entropy Evolution‒Driven: A New Paradigm for Multi‒Domain Fusion Intelligent Cybersecurity
papers.abstract: ObjectiveThe essence of cyberspace security lies in attack-defense games under uncertainty, and the outcome of such games depends on the capability to characterize and control uncertainty. As cyberspace confrontation has extended from the network information domain to the physical domain, electromagnetic spectrum domain, and social cognition domain, uncertainty has increased significantly. The coupling among heterogeneous domains introduces new uncertainty sources and leads to cross-domain propagation and cascading amplification of uncertainty, making confrontation modeling and decision-making increasingly challenging. Traditional single-domain confrontation models are insufficient for characterizing such cross-domain uncertainty propagation. However, existing studies lack a unified uncertainty quantification framework that supports integrated modeling, reasoning, and decision-making for multi-domain fusion confrontation. This paper aimed to establish an entropy-evolution-driven intelligent cybersecurity paradigm, in which multi-domain fusion attack-defense games were characterized as dynamic entropy control processes.MethodsWithin this framework, entropy was introduced as a unified mathematical metric for quantifying heterogeneous uncertainty across multiple domains, and entropy evolution was employed to characterize the dynamic variation of uncertainty states driven by attack-defense interactions. The attack and defense processes were modeled as bidirectional entropy control mechanisms, where both sides attempted to regulate entropy evolution toward favorable states by reducing their own entropy while increasing the opponent entropy. To characterize the uncertainty states underlying entropy evolution, the attack-defense game was modeled from a probabilistic perspective, where the cognitive states of both sides were represented by belief distributions over uncertain environments and opponent strategies. A dual entropy metric framework integrating attack entropy and defense entropy was constructed, where Shannon entropy and relative entropy were incorporated to quantify cognitive uncertainty and characterize attack-defense strategy effectiveness within a unified entropy-based metric framework. The resulting entropy representation provided a common state space for describing the uncertainty evolution of both attack and defense processes, enabling subsequent dynamic analysis and strategic reasoning. Based on the entropy metrics, a cross-domain uncertainty dynamics model was constructed to describe the propagation and amplification of uncertainty among heterogeneous domains under attack-defense interactions. A stochastic difference equation was formulated to characterize entropy evolution, where cross-domain coupling effects were incorporated to capture the cascading transmission of uncertainty. A formal criterion for attack-defense strategy effectiveness was further established through Lyapunov stability theory to evaluate the convergence and stability of entropy evolution under different strategies. This criterion provided a theoretical basis for distinguishing effective strategies from ineffective strategies according to their influence on entropy evolution trajectories. The entropy control logic was further embedded into a game-theoretic reasoning framework to support adaptive attack-defense strategy generation. A hierarchical game-theoretic reasoning model was employed as the underlying reasoning environment, integrating a macroscopic stage-transition model based on Markov decision processes and a microscopic behavior reasoning model based on dynamic Bayesian networks. Based on the dual entropy representation, a belief-driven multi-agent strategy generation method with symmetric opponent modeling was incorporated to characterize both-side cognitive states and generate adaptive strategies under uncertain conditions, forming a closed-loop process among belief updating, entropy evolution, and strategy generation. Through this mechanism, uncertainty quantification, game-theoretic reasoning, and adaptive strategy generation were integrated into a unified computational framework.Results and DiscussionsNumerical reasoning simulations were conducted in a multi-domain security protection scenario of a regional power grid control center to validate the proposed entropy-evolution-driven framework. The results showed that attack entropy and defense entropy transformed heterogeneous uncertainties from the physical, electromagnetic spectrum, network information, and social cognition domains into comparable entropy representations. The analysis of cross-domain coupling effects demonstrated that ignoring uncertainty propagation among domains could lead to pseudo-convergence and misjudgment of strategy effectiveness. Compared with the uncoupled reasoning approach (Baseline A), the proposed method effectively captured the cascading amplification of uncertainty caused by cross-domain interactions and avoided the misjudgment of locally effective but globally ineffective strategies. Compared with the conventional single-domain threshold-based alerting approach (Baseline B), the proposed method enabled more effective defense decisions by integrating multi-domain information fusion, entropy-control objectives, and symmetric opponent modeling. Furthermore, the scenario reasoning demonstrated the closed-loop coupling mechanism between the microscopic-level reasoning process and the macroscopic-level stage transition process in the hierarchical game-theoretic model. The microscopic layer performed belief updating, opponent mirror modeling and reasoning, entropy evolution prediction, and strategy selection within the current confrontation stage, while the resulting entropy evolution provided quantitative criteria for macroscopic-level stage transition. This mechanism enabled the transformation from uncertainty quantification and strategic reasoning to decision-making and stage evolution, forming a unified computational loop for multi-domain fusion confrontation.ConclusionsThe proposed paradigm establishes an entropy-evolution-driven framework for constructing multi-domain fusion cybersecurity architectures. Under this paradigm, defense evolution from kill-chain-oriented operations to kill-web-oriented architectures was interpreted through entropy control, where defensive effectiveness was achieved through coordinated regulation of uncertainty across multiple domains. By integrating entropy-based uncertainty quantification, dynamic modeling, and game-theoretic reasoning, the framework provides a mathematical basis for transforming cyberspace security decision-making from experience-dependent approaches toward computable paradigms. Future research will focus on improving the parameterization of belief distributions and the tractability of entropy computation, advancing the structural identification and parameter acquisition of cross-domain uncertainty dynamics models, and enhancing the real-time scalability of game-theoretic reasoning with large strategy spaces.

papers.title: Next-generation dental implant surface modifications for osseointegration: From nanoengineering to clinical translation.
papers.abstract: This narrative review, prepared in accordance with the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles, surveys next-generation dental implant surface modifications for osseointegration, from nanoengineering to clinical translation. Peri-implantitis affects approximately 19.53% of patients and 12.53% of implants. Because peri-implant tissue destruction reflects a dysregulated host inflammatory response to an unavoidable, lifelong microbial challenge rather than bacterial colonization alone, the design target is shifting from surfaces that are simply bactericidal to surfaces that regulate inflammation while supporting bone integration. Surface design has evolved from machined titanium through sandblasted and acid-etched (SLA) platforms and the superhydrophilic SLActive surface to nanoengineered, bioactive, and stimuli-responsive architectures. SLActive surfaces prevent hydrocarbon adsorption so that near-zero water contact angles are retained, whereas unprotected SLA surfaces progressively lose hydrophilicity with storage time. Electrochemically anodized titanium dioxide nanotube arrays elicit diameter-dependent cellular responses. Tubes with diameters of 70 to 100 nm drive approximately 10-fold elongation of mesenchymal stem cells and selective osteogenic differentiation and enhance bone bonding 9-fold in vivo. Bioactive coatings incorporating nanostructured hydroxyapatite, therapeutic ion-doped bioactive glasses (niobium, cerium, and zinc), and immobilized growth factors such as bone morphogenetic protein 2 and vascular endothelial growth factor actively direct cellular behavior. Antimicrobial strategies, including silver nanoparticles, antimicrobial peptides (GL13K and HHC-36), and photodynamic or photothermal therapies, address microbial colonization while preserving osteogenic potential. However, ensuring lifelong efficacy remains the key challenge for any release-based approach. Stimuli-responsive systems employ pH-responsive gating, zeolitic imidazolate framework-8 metal-organic framework carriers, and enzyme-cleavable linkers to enable microenvironment-triggered release. Additive manufacturing advances, including triply periodic minimal surface lattices and four-dimensional (4D)-printed shape-memory nickel-titanium constructs, enable patient-specific geometries with tailored porosity gradients. In contrast, femtosecond laser texturing, plasma treatments, and atomic layer deposition provide atomic- to micro-scale control. Emerging graphene oxide derivatives, modified polyetheretherketone, and zirconia-based ceramics further broaden the design landscape. Despite robust preclinical evidence, translational progress remains constrained by regulatory complexity, manufacturing scalability, and limited long-term clinical data. Herein, we synthesize preclinical and clinical evidence, identify research gaps, propose artificial intelligence-guided design directions, and outline pathways for translating next-generation surfaces into routine practice. We explicitly outline the limitations inherent to a narrative synthesis.

summary_en.motivation: Peri-implantitis, driven by dysregulated host inflammation, motivates a shift from bactericidal surfaces toward immunomodulatory and osteogenic implant interfaces.
summary_en.method: This SANRA-compliant narrative review traces dental implant surface evolution from machined titanium through SLA/SLActive to nanoengineered, bioactive, stimuli-responsive, and additively manufactured architectures.
summary_en.result: Nanotube arrays, ion-doped bioactive glasses, and antimicrobial strategies show preclinical promise, yet lifelong efficacy, regulatory complexity, and manufacturing scalability constrain translation.
summary_en.validation: Evidence is synthesized from preclinical and clinical literature without original experimental or mechanical testing.
